lesson_title: Debt Flips Everything: Linear Inequalities and Number Lines
hook_text: Why does the inequality sign flip? Because owing R500 is worse than owing R300.
clip_script: Everyone memorises it and nobody believes it — so here is the reason, in money. R500 in your pocket is more than R300 in your pocket. Obvious. Now flip both into debt: you OWE R500, versus you OWE R300. Which is the better position? Owing R300, easily. The bigger number just became the worse position. So five hundred is greater than three hundred, but minus five hundred is LESS than minus three hundred. That is the entire rule. Multiplying or dividing by a negative turns amounts into debts, and the comparison has to flip with them. So minus two x is greater than six becomes x is LESS than minus three. And you never have to trust your memory — test it. Put minus four back into the original: minus two times minus four is eight, and eight beats six. It works. Test the unflipped answer with zero: minus two times zero is zero, which is not bigger than six. It fails. Ten seconds of testing, every time.
visual_style: Two wallets side by side flipping into two debt slips; a number line where 500 and 300 swing across zero and swap order; a quick substitution check ticking green.
mood: Sharp, myth-busting, reassuring at the end.
pacing: Punchy setup on the wallets, a hard flip beat at zero, calm on the test.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for number lines, interval notation and the vetkoek test.
